description: We are building a Space Mission Design Game! Instead of a boring data chart, our goal is to create an engaging, playable game where users experience the real trade-offs of planning a NASA mission—like balancing fuel, budget, payload weight, and launch windows.
summary: We built a space game called Orbital Launchpad: Mars Mission Architect using Base44! Our game solves the Space Mission Design Game challenge by letting players become real flight directors who plan a trip from Earth orbit all the way to Mars. Instead of just flying a rocket, players have to pick the right rocket boosters, pack heavy science tools without exceeding the weight limit, and time their launch window when Earth and Mars line up just right! During the long trip through deep space, players must steer through solar storms, save fuel for orbital insertion, and safely deploy a Mars lander and rover. This game is super important because it teaches kids like us how real NASA rocket scientists plan tricky space flights using math, teamwork, and smart choices. Anyone can learn how hard and exciting it is to send a mission safely into Mars orbit!
details:
1. How Our Game Works

Orbital Launchpad: Mars Mission Architect is an interactive space mission design game built on Base44. Players step into the shoes of a NASA Flight Director at an orbital launchpad high above Earth. Instead of winning by button-mashing, players succeed by making smart engineering choices across four mission stages:

· Stage 1 — Spacecraft & Payload Assembly: Players choose their booster size, fuel tank capacity, solar panels, and science instruments (such as an orbital camera, radar mapper, or surface probe). Every item adds mass! If the rocket is too heavy for the chosen fuel tank, the launchpad computer warns the player to rebalance their design.

· Stage 2 — Planetary Alignment & Launch Window: Earth and Mars orbit the Sun at different speeds. Players watch an animated solar system radar and must press LAUNCH when the two planets reach the green Hohmann transfer window. Launching outside the window wastes fuel and can send the ship into deep space.

· Stage 3 — Interplanetary Cruise & Space Weather: During the 7-month journey to Mars, players manage power and fuel. When a solar flare alert flashes, players must angle their solar panels or turn on radiation shields without draining all their battery power.

· Stage 4 — Mars Orbit Insertion (MOI): Arriving at Mars is super fast! Players must fire their main braking engine at the exact altitude to get captured into a safe orbit around Mars. Too little fuel means flying past Mars; too much thrust risks crashing into the atmosphere.

2. How We Designed It (Ages 5–7)

We started with crayons, paper plates, and building blocks on the classroom floor! We drew Earth and Mars on paper circles to see how a rocket has to aim where Mars WILL be, not where Mars is today. Then we worked with our teacher/mentor to turn our sketches and game rules into a real playable web app.

3. AI Tool Disclosure

Because we are 5 to 7 years old and still learning to read, type, and write computer code, we used AI tools with grown-up supervision to bring our ideas to life:

· Base44 AI App Development Platform: We used Base44 to build the interactive user interface, orbit animations, fuel calculators, and mission feedback screens based on our spoken instructions and drawings.

· AI Writing & Formatting Assistant: Our mentor helped us use an AI writing assistant to turn our spoken explanations into neat, well-spelled sentences for our NASA Space Apps submission documents and slides.

· Human Creativity & Testing: All game concepts, trade-off rules (weight vs. fuel, launch timing, and solar storm shields), visual colors, and playtesting decisions were created by us!
